commenti.body:
I don't believe it's that simple or singular. A society's culture is formed by more than one arena or medium, and most definitely isn't formed by one film.

In regards to the environmental movement, I'd suggest Rachel Carson's *Silent Spring* had a 100 (or 1000) times more influence than Bambi.

Up until the last decade, children's television shows have had the most impact on a generation of kids - at least, more impact than a single film.

Film is definitely part of the influence on society. It's just not the only influence. I also don't think "movement" movies have the same impact as they once did (because of the Internet). However, I do wish certain films had more of an impact. Good Night and Good Luck, Michael Clayton, The Big Short come to mind as "message" movies that could better the future generations. The reality is that children are now more influenced by social media than anything else. Art is losing its power to consumerism and marketing, which is unfortunate (and scary).

The topic interests me because when I grew up in the 80's / 90's prior to the internet, films were an incredibly influential source of 'knowledge.' For instance, I know that war is hell because of film. Platoon, Full Metal Jacket, Apocalypse Now and on and on. 

It stunned me that anyone my age might consider the military post 9/11, for example. 

Films were one of very few portals that could deliver the unvarnished truth about things a curious teen, or anyone really, wanted to know. 

Films were so BIG, too. When a massive pop culture spectacle or Oscar bait film came to town, people talked about them at dinner parties. They were a big deal. 

I feel like film has certainly lost its cultural cachet to the extent that it's considered a lower form of entertainment rather than art that can inform the human experience,  now. 

I find that a loss, because I've always respected film directors as story tellers with an incredibly powerful medium at their disposal and a passion to enrich audiences' lives. 

In the media churn, I don't see that continuing. Killers of the Flower Moon is pretty much forgotten after three weeks. People go, they see, and then they forget.

I hear you, and I agree - films were definitely important to the culture in the previous century. Music was as well. Books even still had an impact.

I have hope that future generations will view the youth from the last decade and the next decade as vapid and cultureless. In response, perhaps it'll be hip to value art again. It's happened before. It can happen again.

Some kids stopped eating meat after watching Babe (1995). There was a study about them, where they are defined as Babe vegetarians. It's a focused effect that can be tracked back to a specific film. Mostly, though, a film's impact (which is greater during one's childhood) are somewhat limited IMO, and if that's a positive or negative impact depends on specific cultures and times.

>In regards to the environmental movement, I'd suggest Rachel Carson's   
>  
>Silent Spring  
>  
> had a 100 (or 1000) times more influence than Bambi.

Man, I disagree with that. Nobody saw *Silent Spring*. *Bambi* was literally seen by every human in western society. 

People really underestimate the power of mainstream film (for better or worse, usually worse in my opinion).

The youth of today are not vapid & cultureless, and to the degree that art has been devalued, it certainly isn’t the kids who are to blame - they didn’t turn movies into “content”, or develop the algorithms that keep us glued to our phones, forever scrolling for ever-elusive validation & connection; or horde their wealth while implementing laws & policies that ensure their children & grandchildren will have to work harder & longer for a much lower quality of life with little or no security or stability; or ban books that tell uncomfortable truths about our history or theatre the fictions on which their power depends: or ignored the science and signs of climate change for decades so that future generations can will be too busy dealing with wildfire seasons that are 12 months long, unprecedented flooding, food shortages, climate refugees, and mass unemployment to give a single f*** whether the kids of today valued art more or less than the generations that came before them.

On a broader scope I think it’s very interesting how people completely lost trust in the government in the US during the 60’s and 70’s and how movies reflected and fuelled that.

WWII movies were a celebration of heroes. Everyone won: the democracy, the government, the soldier and the people. Vietnam movies (and an increased media coverage) became the opposite where everyone lost and it completely shifted the perception of war in peoples minds. People now hated the soldier, the government and realized that democracy was being circumvented at the will of the men in charge. 

It was just a crazy tumultuous time. JFK, MLK, infiltration of the BPP, Watergate and Nixon, Covert CIA ops in third world countries, MK Ultra and so on. 

I think Hollywood played such a huge role in how the world saw their governments. It was really a generation of conflicted filmmakers that made these movies in the 70’s. All the conspiracy movies and Vietnam films like The Deer Hunter, Apocalypse Now and Full Metal Jacket contributed to that.

In the 80’s Hollywood gave birth to the blockbuster culture and slowly the narrative shifted. It became more about the individual’s journey. 

Conspiracy films now focused on the corporations instead of the government and we’ve largely been in that space since then.

Silent Spring was a book of the month club selection back when that meant something.  It arrived in American homes like a bombshell.  The author spoke before Congress and the book lead directly to the creation of the EPA.  Its impact was profound and long lasting.  I can’t think of any lasting effect of Bambi other than a generation of stripper names.

Oh boy. I knew there'd be at least one person who would take offense, taking a general statement as a personal insult. For the record, I didn't blame the youth for anything. To be clear, I mostly blame the complete dominance of consumerism and marketing for these generations being vapid and cultureless.

You touched on that yourself, so I can only assume you're working hard to solve that societal problem so future generations of youths don't have to be victimized by it (especially since that AI is going to take over that arena).

You desperately need knowledge and perspective if you actually believe all those things you typed. Read about history, and perhaps talk to your grandparents about their parents and grandparents. That should cover the last 100 years. You might not be able to understand all the information until you're 25, 30, or 35, but take it all in and try. I mean, just for starters, you should learn about the Depression Era, with its unprecedented droughts, food shortages, and mass unemployment - its low quality of life, lack of security and stability. If you want to play the suffering olympics between the generations, you're going to at least lose to that one.

>I don't believe it's that simple or singular. A society's culture is formed by more than one arena or medium, and most definitely isn't formed by one film.

I agree; we're talking about something extremely complex.

Why, exactly? Honest question. 

(and I didn't downvote you, though I probably should because it's a lazy response)

I think when some controversial or progressive subject matter is covered intelligently, when it's done in a subtle way, when it feels natural, that will resonate with viewers and has a chance to change their mind or at least their perspective on an issue.

When it feels forced, when you can sense that the producers or director felt obligated to go along with the latest societal norms and force or shoehorn the material in instead of having it develop organically or incidentally to the plot then it can often have the opposite effect with viewers because they feel like they are being preached to, they lose immersion from the story and instead dig their heels in further on the issue and steel themselves for the next time someone tries to change their mind.

Well, because of your confidence while being so ignorant. First, as someone else pointed out, Silent Spring was a book - Rachel Carson was the author. Second, you don't know the meaning of "literally." Third, why would stating what most of western civilization knows (that Carson's book had a far more impact on the environmental movement than the film Bambi) equate to underestimating mainstream film?

How very mature of you, good god. 

I know what the book is and its influence. However, its influence was mostly in academic circles and some book clubs, which is very different than pretty much every single person on the face of the Earth seeing *Bambi*.

Both things are influential, but the impact of messaging in mainstream culture is constantly underestimated.
You're not only an idiot, but a liar as well. Best of luck.

You’re certainly right that more people experienced Bambi than Silent Spring. But you’ve done nothing to even sketch a hypothetical as to how the Disney film might have influenced public policy. While r/badwhiskey63 has laid out some facts about Silent Spring’s concrete effect. It’s all very fine to say a billion kids shed a tear for the deer. But to claim any effect on the physical world, you’d have to do better than that
